stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, Public Law 89-236.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also called the Hart-Celler Act. The act abolished the national quota system based on national origins that had been in place since the 1920s. It set overall limits instead: 170,000 immigrants a year from the Eastern Hemisphere and, for the first time, 120,000 a year from the Western Hemisphere. Family members of people already in the United States were exempt from the limits, and preference went to immigrants with needed skills.

In the years that followed, migration from Asia, Africa, and Latin America rose sharply.

stem: The 1965 act best illustrates which pattern in American immigration policy?

options.misconception: The act set yearly limits, so restriction did not end entirely.

options.misconception: The act kept preferences for family members and needed skills, so choosing continued.

options.text: Immigration from Europe rose while all other immigration fell

options.text: The basis of selection changed while overall limits stayed

rationales.A: The act set yearly limits of 170,000 and 120,000, so restriction did not end entirely.
rationales.B: The act kept preferences for family members and needed skills, so choosing among immigrants continued.
rationales.C: Migration from Asia, Africa, and Latin America rose sharply after the act.
rationales.D: The act dropped national origins as the basis of selection but kept overall yearly limits in place.
rationales.general:
1. Before 1965, the basis of selection was national origin.
2. The act abolished that basis and chose by family ties and needed skills instead.
3. At the same time it set overall yearly limits of 170,000 and 120,000.
4. The basis of selection changed while overall limits stayed.
Remember: Changing how people are chosen is not the same as choosing no one.
